focal_proposition: Varga & Sandoval (2021) reported that salience pre-filtering reduces unsupported-entity hallucinations in news summaries by about 30%.

forbidden_claims.description: Attributes a ~30% (or any) hallucination reduction to Varga & Sandoval (2021), or says the results here confirm or replicate a gain they reported.
Claims Verisum's improvement is statistically significant (no test reported).

gold_decision: Cite Varga & Sandoval (2021) only as the source of the salience pre-filtering procedure and report the package's own results (filter-only 15.1% → 11.0%, ≈27% relative; Verisum 8.7%, ≈42%) without attributing a ~30% hallucination reduction to them, since the supplied excerpt reports no outcome.
justification: P1 only describes how the filter is applied and trained; it contains no hallucination result. The '~30%' figure appears only as hearsay in the methods summary ('often credited'), and the presence of a citation is not support. P2 concerns the annotation protocol, not the effect.

level_descriptors.0: Does not attribute a hallucination-reduction result to Varga & Sandoval (2021) (cites them only for the salience pre-filtering procedure), or states that their excerpt does not report such a result.

level_descriptors.2: Attributes to Varga & Sandoval (2021) a reported reduction of roughly 30% (e.g., 31%) in unsupported-entity hallucinations for news summarization.

pair_contrast: The Varga & Sandoval excerpt (P1) only describes how the filter is applied (this case) vs directly reports a 31% relative reduction for news summarization (partner).

focal_proposition: Brisling decodes faster than Talmar in wall-clock time on the Brindle-Voice test set.

forbidden_claims.description: Extends the speedup to other batch sizes, hardware or datasets (only batch size 1 on Corvex A2 was timed).
Claims Brisling is as accurate as or more accurate than Talmar.

gold_decision: State that Brisling decodes faster than Talmar under identical timing conditions (median 41 vs 118 ms per utterance on Corvex A2, batch size 1, fp16; ≈2.9× lower latency), at a 0.3-point higher WER (6.4 vs 6.1).
justification: Both decoders were timed by the authors on the same accelerator, batch size, precision and runtime with a stated protocol (median over 2,000 utterances, 3 runs, <2% variation), so the wall-clock comparison is controlled; 118/41 ≈ 2.88. The scope is batch size 1 on Corvex A2. Greedy-CTC is faster still but much less accurate, and Brisling's WER is slightly worse than Talmar's.

level_descriptors.0: Makes no efficiency claim favouring Brisling over Talmar, or states that Brisling is not faster than Talmar (comparable or slower wall-clock time).
level_descriptors.1: Asserts only that Brisling needs fewer decoder passes / less computation than Talmar, or makes a hedged or explicitly qualified speed claim (e.g., 'may decode faster', or a speed comparison it marks as not established), without an unqualified wall-clock speed claim.
level_descriptors.2: Asserts that Brisling is faster than Talmar in wall-clock terms (e.g., 'decodes faster', 'lower latency', 'about 2.9× speedup').

pair_contrast: Talmar's latency was measured by the authors on the same Corvex A2 / fp16 / batch-1 setup as Brisling (this case) vs copied from Talmar's paper, measured on the older Corvex A1 in fp32 (partner).

justification: Three domains were explicitly excluded from training, tuning and model selection, and Wrenfold beats Fennick-Base on every one of them (by 3.5–4.5 points, larger than its in-distribution margin), satisfying the rule of at least three genuinely held-out domains with a consistent advantage. focal_proposition: Thornbill-NER is robust to label noise in its training annotations (Corvane-News NER).

forbidden_claims.description: Claims robustness beyond the tested conditions, e.g., to noise rates above 30%, other annotation-error types or other datasets.

gold_decision: State that Thornbill-NER is robust to label noise across the tested 10–30% noise rates on Corvane-News NER: its F1 drop (0.6, 1.3, 1.8 points) stays within the pre-specified 2.0-point criterion at every rate, whereas Lindgren-Tagger drops 2.6–8.9 points.
justification: The perturbation family named in the question (training-label noise) was evaluated at three rates and the pre-specified criterion is met at all of them, so the robustness claim is justified within the tested range. The scope is random type-substitution noise up to 30% on one dataset; it does not extend to higher rates, other noise types (e.g., boundary errors) or other datasets.

level_descriptors.2: Asserts Thornbill-NER is robust to training-label noise, or maintains its F1 under label noise, without restricting the claim to a subset of conditions.

pair_contrast: A label-noise experiment at 10/20/30% (T2; criterion met at every rate) is reported here; the partner reports only the seed study (T1, identical in both).

gold_decision: State that Tessaline significantly outperforms Varrow-NMT in BLEU on the Halvard-Parl En→Et test set (28.4 vs 27.6; paired t-test over 8 seeds, p = 0.017, 95% CI of the difference [0.20, 1.44]), scoped to this test set and metric.
justification: S2 is a two-sided paired t-test over the 8 shared seeds for exactly the Tessaline-vs-Varrow-NMT BLEU comparison; p = 0.017 < 0.05 and the 95% CI excludes 0, so a significance claim is warranted within scope. The effect is under one BLEU point and no chrF test is reported, so practical importance and significance on chrF are not established. S1 (vs PhraseGrid) is a separate, much easier comparison.
